hypothesis: The eggNOG orthologous group ENOG410XSU2 (endoribonuclease L-PSP / RidA-family protein) is increased or characteristic in 12-month-old infants receiving dairy-based complementary protein relative to those receiving meat-based complementary protein.
rationale: Searches combining the feature name, its eggNOG identifier, and the exposure keywords (dairy vs. meat complementary protein, infant gut microbiome/metagenome, weaning) returned no study - human or animal - that reports this orthologous group, or the endoribonuclease L-PSP/RidA (YjgF/YER057c/UK114, PF01042) protein family, as differentially abundant between dairy-fed and meat-fed infants, or between any contrasting dietary protein sources in the gut. What was found is: (i) primary trial literature on the exact exposure contrast (the Denver randomized controlled feeding trial of meat- vs. dairy-based complementary foods in U.S. formula-fed infants from 5 to 12 months), which reports taxonomic differences (e.g., genus-level shifts, Ruminococcus/Roseburia and SCFA-related findings) but no report of this gene family; and (ii) a companion metagenomic/metabolomic network-representation-learning analysis of the same trial, whose abstract-level content describes diet-associated microbiome and metabolite features but which did not surface any statement about endoribonuclease L-PSP in the retrievable text; and (iii) a substantial mechanistic literature on RidA/L-PSP proteins as 2-aminoacrylate/enamine-imine deaminases that protect PLP-dependent enzymes (e.g., threonine/serine dehydratase) during amino acid metabolism, which provides only generic, theoretical reasoning that a high-protein, milk-protein-rich diet could increase amino-acid-catabolism-associated housekeeping functions. This is pathway-level/theoretical support only, with nothing tying the feature to the dairy arm specifically, and the direction is equally plausible for a meat-based (also high-protein) diet. That situation maps to a score of 1 (weak, generic reasoning only) rather than 0 (nothing relevant found) or -1 (no study reported the opposite direction for this feature either). Additional caution: the eggNOG annotation is labeled 'function unknown', the L-PSP/RidA family is a broadly conserved housekeeping family present across most bacterial genomes, and its metagenomic abundance is likely to track overall taxonomic composition rather than diet per se.

evidence.title: Different gut microbiota in U.S. formula-fed infants consuming a meat vs. dairy-based complementary foods: A randomized controlled trial
evidence.study_population: Full-term, formula-fed U.S. infants (metro Denver) randomized to meat- or dairy-based complementary foods from ~5 to 12 months of age
evidence.relevance: Primary study of the exact exposure contrast and age window in the hypothesis; establishes that diet-group differences in the infant gut microbiota exist at 12 months, but the reported differences are taxonomic (e.g., genus-level shifts) and the retrievable text contains no mention of endoribonuclease L-PSP/RidA or any eggNOG functional ortholog - i.e., it neither supports nor contradicts the feature-specific hypothesis.

evidence.title: Network-based representation learning reveals the impact of age and diet on the gut microbial and metabolomic environment of U.S. infants in a randomized controlled feeding trial
evidence.study_population: U.S. formula-fed infants, 5-12 months, randomized to meat- vs. dairy-based complementary diet; fecal metagenomics and metabolomics
evidence.relevance: The most directly relevant functional-metagenomics analysis of this exposure; describes diet- and age-associated microbiome/metabolite features (with the meat group described as enriched for certain features), but no statement about ENOG410XSU2 or endoribonuclease L-PSP was retrievable, so it provides context rather than direct support for the hypothesized dairy-associated increase.

evidence.title: RidA Proteins Protect against Metabolic Damage by Reactive Intermediates
evidence.study_population: Review of bacterial (Salmonella enterica and other prokaryote) and eukaryotic model systems; not infants
evidence.relevance: Defines the biological role of the endoribonuclease L-PSP/RidA (YjgF/YER057c/UK114) family as enamine/imine deaminases quenching 2-aminoacrylate generated by PLP-dependent amino acid dehydratases; supplies only generic, pathway-level reasoning that could link this family to dietary amino acid load, with no diet-group or infant-specific direction.

evidence.title: Integrated Metabolomics and Transcriptomics Suggest the Global Metabolic Response to 2-Aminoacrylate Stress in Salmonella enterica
evidence.study_population: Salmonella enterica in vitro (bacterial model system)
evidence.relevance: Primary mechanistic study showing that loss of the RidA (2-iminobutanoate/2-iminopropanoate deaminase, EC 3.5.99.10) function perturbs amino acid metabolism; supports the plausibility that this gene family relates to microbial amino acid catabolism but says nothing about dairy vs. meat protein or infant gut communities.

evidence.title: Different Blood Metabolomics Profiles in Infants Consuming a Meat- or Dairy-Based Complementary Diet
evidence.study_population: Infants in the same meat- vs. dairy-based complementary feeding controlled trial, 5-12 months with 24-month follow-up (serum metabolomics)
evidence.relevance: Shows the dairy vs. meat contrast produces measurable amino-acid-related metabolic differences in infants, which is the only indirect thread connecting this exposure to amino-acid-metabolism-associated microbial functions; it does not measure microbial gene families and thus does not test the hypothesis.

caveats: The feature is an eggNOG ortholog group annotated 'function unknown' whose named homolog family (endoribonuclease L-PSP / RidA / YjgF-like, PF01042) is a near-ubiquitous bacterial housekeeping family; differential abundance in shotgun metagenomes is therefore likely to reflect underlying taxonomic turnover (e.g., Proteobacteria/Bacteroidetes vs. Bifidobacterium proportions) rather than a diet-specific functional adaptation, and the eggNOG ID itself is not indexed in the biomedical literature. Search coverage was also limited by a tool-call quota, so a small number of planned follow-up queries (e.g., '"endoribonuclease L-PSP" infant', metaproteomic dairy-protein queries) could not be executed; a full-text search of the meat-vs-dairy trial's metagenomic supplementary tables would be the decisive next step.
